1.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [while I was suffering]

2.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please deliver my soul]

The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent himself as a whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [from those who speak lies]

The psalmist is using is using parts of a person, **lips** and **tongue** to represent his enemies who are telling lies about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from people speaking falsehood and deceit about me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from those who speak falsely]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from those who deceive]

3.note: The psalmist is using the question form to warn his enemies of certain punishment from God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this question as a statement or as exclamation. Alternate translation: [He will give punishment to you, and he will add more to you]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [What severe punishment will he give to you]
The pronoun **he** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will Yahweh give]

As in the previous verse, **tongue of deceit** represents the psalmist’s enemies who are telling lies about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [O you who speak deceitfully]

4.q: חִצֵּ֣י גִבּ֣וֹר שְׁנוּנִ֑ים עִ֝֗ם גַּחֲלֵ֥י רְתָמִֽים
4.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context of the previous verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He will give you arrows of a warrior, sharpened, with coals of broom trees]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh’s punishment were **arrows of a warrior, sharpened**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Severe punishment]

The expression **sharpened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that someone has sharpened]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s punishment were **coals of broom trees**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [burning destruction]

5.note: The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, distress, about his situation. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the psalmist was feeling. Alternate translation: [How miserable I am]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The places named both refer to the people who lived in those places who were considered barbarian or savage. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I have lived for a long time among hostile people]

Here, **the tents of Kedar** represents the people who live in those tents. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Kedar]

6.note: The psalmist is using **My soul** to represent himself as a whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have dwelt for a long time]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those who hate to live peacefully]

7.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I am for peace]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [am someone who wants to live peacefully]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but when I speak about peace]

The psalmist uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between his peaceful disposition and his neighbors’ desire for conflict. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and yet when]
The pronoun **they** refers to those who hate peace mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those people are for war]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **war**, you could express the same idea in another way as is modeled in the UST.
